summary: Depending on definition, roughly 20-35% of US adults report muscle-strengthening activity >=2x/week (NHIS 2020: men 35%, women 27%; ages 18-44 men 44.5%/women 34%, falling to 22%/17% at 65+), and ~58% do none at all; worldwide pooled ~23%, Europe ~17% (Nordic 34-52%, SE Europe <8%), Australia ~10%. Weight training specifically is clearly lower: Gallup found 27% of Americans lift at least weekly and only 15% 3+x/week, and England's stricter deliberate-strengthening definition roughly halves prevalence (men 29%->16%, women 24%->9%). A reasonable model is that ~15-25% of young-adult men and ~8-15% of young-adult women train with weights regularly, declining with age. Population grip norms (Dodds 2014: median peak ~51 kg men, ~31 kg women; PURE: men <40 Europe/N. America median 50 kg, IQR 43-56) give a general-strength anchor; physically active non-lifters such as light manual workers are only modestly stronger than office workers (~12% in grip), and the occupational effect is inconsistent across studies, so non-lifters cluster near the general-population distribution rather than near lifters.
